## Paper

## Abstract

Sea level rise is expected to cause chronic shoreline retreat, affecting over 10% of the world’s population in low-elevation coastal zones (LECZ). Sandy beaches supported by man-made structures are more vulnerable to substantial beach area loss due to restricted landward migration, affecting ecosystem services. However, the global extent of ‘hardened’ sandy coastlines at risk of ‘severe beach loss’ has not been comprehensively quantified. Here, using products and geospatial datasets derived from satellite imagery, we find that, 33% of the world’s sandy coastline is currently hardened. Analysis of the results by IPCC AR6 regions show that the most hardened coastal regions are the Bay of Bengal, Western & Central Europe, the Mediterranean, Western North America, and East Asia. Linking coastal hardening information with existing shoreline retreat projections, we find that under SSP5-8.5, up to 26% of the world’s sandy coastline (~52,100 km) is likely to face severe beach loss by the end of the 21st century. Under a moderate emissions scenario (SSP2-4.5), this projection decreases to 21% (~42,080 km), highlighting the potential mitigation gain. The results also show that the vast majority of projected severe sandy beach losses are in high and upper-middle-income countries, with up to 82% of severe losses under SSP5-8.5 and up to 81% under SSP2-4.5 by the end of the 21st century, relative to the total length of sandy coastline, including both hardened and natural coastlines. The IPCC AR6 regions with the highest projected sandy beach losses include Eastern North America, Northern South America, the Mediterranean, the Bay of Bengal, Western Africa, and South-east Asia.

---

## Introduction

Changes in climatic and non-climatic impact drivers are projected to lead to shoreline retreat around the world during the 21st century, in the absence of abundant sand supply to the coast and/or any physical obstruction to shoreline retreat1,2. In a first-pass assessment of global shoreline changes over the 21st century, Vousdoukas et al.3 projects that under a high emission scenario (RCP 8.5), ~50% of the global sandy coastline could face severe erosion (defined therein as a chronic shoreline retreat exceeding 100 m) by the end of the century. Given that ~10% of the global population currently lives in low-elevation coastal areas (i.e., <10m above MSL), a number that is projected to increase by up to 11.6% by 20504, such severe shoreline retreat is likely to lead to substantial socio-economic impacts. In an earlier study, Hinkel et al.5 estimated the economic cost of forced migration due to sea level rise-driven coastal erosion over the 21st century to be around US$ 1 Trillion. However, none of the aforementioned global shoreline change studies account for the currently existing physical obstructions (such as seawalls, harbor structures, highway and railway revetments) to sandy shoreline retreat, let alone the likely increase of such infrastructure in the coming decades.

Given the rapid increase in population migration to coastal zones since the 1950s6, inevitably leading to large-scale coastal developments that need protection against coastal erosion and flooding, a substantial proportion of the world’s sandy coastline is “hardened” by gray infrastructure. Considering such “hardened coasts” in shoreline retreat assessments is important for at least two reasons: (1) where hardened coasts are present and maintained, shoreline retreat could, at most, occur until the physical obstruction is reached. Projections that assume no physical obstructions to shoreline retreat (as is the case in Hinkel et al.5 and Vousdoukas et al.3), may therefore substantially overpredict the retreat amount at these locations; (2) sandy beaches that have unlimited backshore accommodation space may translate landward as a whole in response to sea level rise7, maintaining their width even as the shoreline retreats. In these latter cases, shoreline retreat need not necessarily result in beach area loss. Whether the projected rate of accelerated SLR beyond mid-century could outpace the rate of landward beach translation is not yet known. However, beaches that are backed by maintained structures could be unable to translate landward, and such beaches may eventually be eroded completely8,9. Indeed, beach loss can already be seen in front of many seawalls around the world. For instance, the entire sandy beach in front of a revetment constructed in Santa Cruz was eroded under wave action10. Along the Atlantic coast’s barrier islands, as well as along the coasts of Oahu, and the states of California and Washington, the process of gradual beach loss in front of the seawall or revetment together with the landward migration of the shoreline has been well documented10–13. Given that sea levels are projected to rise for centuries, even if greenhouse gas emissions are sharply reduced immediately14, sandy beaches fronting hardened coastlines are likely to eventually be lost unless local remedies such as sand nourishments are implemented, or unless there is an ample natural supply of sand to the coast (e.g., via fluvial sediment supply, sand supply from the lower shoreface). To date, studies on coastal hardening have been limited to specific countries or environments. For example, Gittman, et al.15 show that up to 14% of the US coastline (all shoreline types) is hardened. Major coastal cities such as New York, San Diego, Sydney, and Hong Kong currently have 50% or more of their shorelines hardened15–20. A comprehensive global-scale assessment of the number of sandy beaches that are backed by gray infrastructure has hitherto not been undertaken, and consequently, due to the reasons discussed above, the longevity of such beaches remains unknown.

In this work, we aim to answer three specific questions: (1) how much of the global sandy coastline has been artificially hardened? (2) how much of the global sandy coastline is likely to face severe beach loss by the mid- and end-21st century under moderate (SSP2-4.5) and high (SSP5-8.5) emission scenarios? and (3) Which parts of the world are at high risk of facing severe sandy beach loss? In this study, “gray infrastructure” or “hardening” refers to rigid human-made (semi-) impermeable structures that alter the natural landscape, and potentially obstruct shoreline retreat and landward translation of sandy beaches. This includes impervious surfaces such as roads, highways, railways, buildings, and other urbanized developments, which even if they are not resilient enough against erosion in their current form, are valuable assets that are likely to be further protected by engineering structures when they are facing imminent damage, thus obstructing shoreline retreat and landward translation of beaches well into the future.

---

## Results

Hardened sandy beaches
Using GISA-10m in conjunction with the infrastructure data from OSM, we quantified the amount of hardened sandy coast length worldwide. Our results show that 33% (based on GISA-10m plus OSM) world’s sandy coastline is currently hardened (see the text box in Fig. 1a), losing the natural adaptability to accommodate future sea level rise, and is therefore more prone to experience beach loss as the shoreline retreats. At the regional scale, Fig. 1a shows the percentage of hardened sandy coastline in each IPCC AR6 region. The top 5 regions for coastal hardening (in descending order of percentage of sandy coastline hardened in the region) are the Bay of Bengal (84%), Western & Central Europe (68%), the Mediterranean (65%), Western North America (61%), and East Asia (50%). The IPCC AR6 regions with the lowest percentages of artificial hardening are Central Australia (5%), North-eastern North America (5%), North-Eastern Africa (5%), North Australia (3%), and Madagascar (3%). Interestingly, of the top 5 hardened regions, only Western & Central Europe has a noteworthy (>5km2/km) LECZ area per kilometer length of coastline, indicating that the mere presence of large LECZ may not be a driver for coastal hardening (Supplementary Table 524,26,27). However, all of the above top 5 hardened regions are affected by medium to high degrees of storminess, based on the integrated storm wave energy and frequency index28. In addition, most of these regions contain high-income and upper-middle-income countries with major seaports where coastal infrastructure investment can be high, necessitating their protection with engineering structures29. In the Bay of Bengal and the Mediterranean, the population in coastal zones (i.e., within 100 km from the coast) is high (more than 50%–75% of the total population)30, likely making coastal protection a management priority.

The global estimated erodible beach width along hardened coasts, representing the distance from the shoreline to the nearest artificial structure, is 93 m [4 m–497 m] (median [5th–95th percentiles]) (See ‘Global’ boxplot in Fig. 1b). When regions are ordered (lowest to highest) based on the median erodible beach width, artificial structures are found closest to the shoreline in the Northern South America region (Fig. 1b), followed by the Caribbean, Southern Australia, Western Africa, and New Zealand—all within a regionally averaged 56 m from the shoreline. The regions with the widest erodible sandy beaches are found in North-Eastern North America, North-Western South America, Central Australia, South Asia, and North-Eastern Africa (lowest to highest).

Severe sandy beach loss projections
We combine our coastal hardening results with Vousdoukas et al.’s3 shoreline retreat projections to estimate the severe sandy beach loss projections by the middle and end of the 21st century under RCP4.5 (comparable to SSP2-4.5) and RCP8.5 (comparable to SSP5-8.5). We considered all shoreline retreats >100 m at hardened sandy locations to be indicative of potential severe beach loss, in line with Vousdoukas et al.’s3 definition of severe erosion (see Methods). This threshold choice is further supported by the current median global erodible hardened sandy beach width of 93 m derived above from GISA-10m plus OSM (See ‘Global’ box plot in Fig. 1b). Here, we also included locations where the shoreline retreat is less than 100 m but greater than or equal to the distance from present-day shoreline to the nearest gray infrastructure, as these indicate near-complete beach loss. We find that under SSP2-4.5, 4%–15% (5th–95th percentile range) of the world’s sandy coastline could face severe beach loss by mid-century, increasing to 9%–21% by the end of the 21st century (see text boxes in Fig. 2). Under SSP5-8.5, severe sandy beach loss is projected to occur at 4%–19% of sandy coasts by mid-21st century, increasing to 9%–26% by the end of the 21st century (note: percentages indicate the proportion of the global sandy coastline that is projected to experience severe beach loss, here defined as hardened locations where projected shoreline retreat is more than 100 m, or hardened locations where projected shoreline retreat is less than 100 m but is equal to or greater than the distance from the present-day shoreline to the nearest artificial structure). The median projections, statistically representing the most likely or expected value, show that 7% of the world’s sandy coastline could face severe beach loss by mid-century under SSP2-4.5, increasing to 8% under SSP5-8.5. By the end of the 21st century, the most likely projections are 14% under SSP2-4.5 and 19% under SSP5-8.5. Of only the hardened sandy coasts, by mid-century, 20% [11%–43%] are projected to face severe beach loss under SSP2-4.5, increasing to 23% [10%–55%] under SSP5-8.5. By the end-century, 42% [24%–63%] and 55% [27%–78%] of the hardened sandy coasts are projected to face severe beach loss under SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5, respectively.

Geographically, most sandy beaches under threat are located in Eastern North America, Northern South America, Mediterranean, Bay of Bengal, Western Africa, and South-East Asia regions (Fig. 2). In Eastern North America, under SSP2-4.5, 29% [19%–32%] of the regional sandy coastline is projected to suffer severe beach loss by mid-century, this percentage remaining unchanged till the end-century (Supplementary Table 1). Under SSP5-8.5, the mid-century projection for this region increases to 30% [17%–33%], while the end-century projection increases to 31% [26%–33%]. In Northern South America, 21% [11%–28%] of the sandy coastline is projected to experience severe beach loss under SSP2-4.5 by mid-century, and 22% [16%–28%] by end-century. Under SSP5-8.5, the severe beach loss percentage is projected to increase to 22% [10%–30%] by mid-century, and to 24% [17%–29%] by end-century. In Mediterranean, 20% [8%–38%] of the sandy coastline is projected to face severe beach loss under SSP2-4.5 by mid-century, and 37% [24%–48%] by end-century. Under SSP5-8.5, these projections increase to 24% [8%–44%] for mid-century, and to 44% [26%–54%] for the end of the century. In the Bay-of-Bengal, under SSP2-4.5, 13% [9%–23%] of the sandy coastline is projected to suffer severe beach loss by mid-century, and 34% [20%–58%] by end-century. Under SSP5-8.5, the mid-century projection for this region increases to 15% [10%–41%] by mid-century, while the end-century projection increases to 49% [21%–74%]. (The regional distribution of severe beach loss as % of only the hardened sandy coast line is given in Supplementary Table 2).

Fig. 2 indicates that transitioning from high to moderate emissions could yield a more substantial impact at the end of the century compared to mid-century. Although there is no discernible difference in the sandy coastline length at risk resulting from the shift from SSP5-8.5 to SSP2-4.5 by mid-century, this mitigation strategy exhibits potential reductions of up to 5% representing ~10,020 km of sandy coast by the end-century. Similar observations hold at the regional level, where the benefits are more pronounced in the long term than in the near future, with projections indicating a maximum reduction of ~5% in the sandy coastline length that could experience severe beach loss from the SSP5-8.5 to SSP2-4.5 transition (Supplementary Table 1). Bay of Bengal, Western & Central Europe, Western North America, Eastern Australia, South-Eastern South America, and North-Eastern South America are the regions projected to benefit the most from mitigation. Fig. 2 also shows that, in general, projected sandy beach losses are highest in regions with a high level of coastline hardening. However, it is important to note that this does not imply that coastline hardening is the sole direct cause of beach loss, as our definition of severe beach loss is strongly influenced by both shoreline retreat projections and the available erodible beach width.

Socio-economic dimensions of the findings
We further included country income in our analysis to investigate the socio-economic dimensions of our findings on coastal hardening and severe beach loss. By examining these aspects through the lens of country income status, we can determine whether extensive infrastructure investments in high-income countries inadvertently result in maladaptation. Considering the World Bank’s classification of income groups by 2022 gross national income (GNI) per capita—low income (≤$1135), lower-middle-income ($1136 to $4465), upper-middle-income ($4466 to $13,845), and high income (≥$13,846)29—, we find that 56% of the global hardened sandy coasts are found in high-income countries, 26% in upper-middle-income countries, 15% in lower-middle-income countries, and only 3% in low-income countries (Fig. 3a). By mid-century, the majority of severe beach loss is projected to occur in high-income and upper-middle-income countries under both emission scenarios considered (81% [76%–83%]) (Fig. 3b and Supplementary Table 3). There were no major changes to these mid-century projections by the end of the century.

The largest share of hardened coastlines and sandy beaches facing severe beach loss in high-income countries primarily reflects the fact that higher-income countries are more likely to have the resources to invest in and maintain coastal hardening structures, which, as our results show, may lead to unintended consequences and higher beach losses in future. It should be noted that the correlation between income groups and severe beach loss is a finding from our analysis and is not related to how shoreline retreat was computed by Vousdoukas et al.3, as their analysis does not consider shoreline hardening. It is important to acknowledge the potential underestimation in the percentage of hardened sandy beaches and, consequently, in the percentage of sandy beaches facing severe loss in low and lower-middle-income countries due to the higher possibility of unmapped areas in community-based OSM data. This limitation should be borne in mind when interpreting Fig. 3.

Considering the current projections of higher population and urbanization in coastal zones over the 21st century31,32, the development of critical infrastructure or coastal protection measures is expected to increase proportionally. This underscores the potential for even more sandy beach losses than our current estimate, which does not account for any future changes in coastal hardening.

---

## Methods

Data
SDS. We used an updated version of Luijendijk et al.’s33 Satellite-Derived Shorelines (SDS) dataset to locate sandy beach locations. In this dataset, sandy beaches are detected based on supervised pixel classification of Sentinel-2 imagery at 500 m spaced transects orthogonal to the global shoreline from the OSM dataset of 2016. In the preprocessing step, we removed contentious data points (i.e., points that the original SDS dataset categorizes as ‘sandy’ when they are not sandy and vice versa) from the original SDS dataset based on cross-checks with Google Earth satellite imagery. Whatever non-rocky cliffs (e.g., sandstone) may have remained in Luijendijk et al.’s33 SDS classifications would also have been included in our analysis. Most of these removed data points were located on the Canadian east and west coasts, the south coast of Chile, the coastline of Guyana, small island nations in the South Pacific, and the Indian Ocean (including the Solomon Islands, Vanuatu, and New Caledonia), and the Lesser Antilles. Overall, this resulted in 25% fewer locations compared to the original SDS dataset. The final sandy location dataset contains 1,053,613 data points.

GISA. We used three versions of the GISA dataset: (1) Version 1.0 at 30m resolution (GISA-30m-V1)21; (2) Version 2.0 at 30m resolution (GISA-30m-V2)23; (3) Version 3.0 at 10m resolution (GISA-10m)22. We emphasize here the results based on GISA-10m since it is reported to have an accuracy >86%. GISA-10m is derived from over 2.7 million Sentinel optical and radar images. It was generated using 58 million training samples extracted through temporal, spatial, spectral, and geometric rules on various sources of geospatial datasets. In addition to its higher resolution, it has the added benefit of detecting transportation networks resulting from the integration of OSM data in training samples for classification. Therefore, GISA-10m is particularly well suited for our study as it captures coastal structures and revetments along highways and railway that could impede shoreline retreat and beach translation. We used GISA-30m-V1 and GISA-30m-V2 only to test the sensitivity of our results to different spatial resolutions and image classification techniques. The details of GISA-30m-V1 and GISA-30m-V2, along with associated results, are discussed in the “Sensitivity of severe sandy beach loss percentage on GISA versions and spatial resolutions” section of the Supplementary Information.

OSM. We used the community-built global geospatial OSM24 in conjunction with the GISA data to rectify any imagery misclassifications. Although GISA-10m has integrated information from OSM into its training samples, it still has lower accuracy in rural and arid areas. Through manual inspection, we identified a few misclassifications of sandy beaches as urbanized pixels. Therefore, to more accurately define hardened sandy beaches, we incorporated infrastructure data from OSM to establish the ‘hardened’ classification. Specifically, we utilized OSM keys ‘building’, ‘land use’, ‘highway’, and ‘railway’ (Supplementary Table 4). OSM attributes that did not align with a gray infrastructure definition were filtered out manually.

Global shoreline retreat projections. In this study, we used Vousdoukas et al.’s3 projections of chronic shoreline retreat due to the combined effects of Relative SLR (R) and ambient changes (AC) at mid- and end-21st century under RCP4.5 and 8.5 scenarios. Several previous studies have suggested such addition of the RSLR-driven and ambient contributions to net shoreline change to estimate the total future shoreline change34,35. Vousdoukas et al.3 dataset provide projections of shoreline retreat for sandy locations globally at 500 m alongshore resolution. R is estimated using an improved version of the Bruun Rule36 with a correction for its known overestimation compared to projections from physics-based models. The ambient changes, which are added to the RSLR-driven shoreline retreat, essentially represent the manifestation of all other background processes, such as fluvial sediment supply, headland bypassing, lower shoreface transport, etc., on shoreline position change. AC was obtained from historical shoreline change rates (1984-2016) reported by Luijendijk, et al.29 and Mentaschi et al.37, also at 500 m alongshore spacing. It should be noted that these projections do not account for physical obstructions to shoreline retreat (e.g., seawalls, revetments), an aspect explicitly addressed in our study (please see “Hardened sandy beaches” in Methods).

Computational framework
Our analysis covers 1,053,613 locations spaced at 500 m along the ice-free global coastline. First, we verified whether the coast location of interest is sandy using the updated SDS data. If confirmed as sandy, we then examined the presence (or not) of an artificial structure within the corresponding backshore search area, leveraging information from both GISA and OSM. If an artificial structure is identified, the sandy location is classified as hardened, and shoreline retreat projections are integrated into the analysis, followed by a further assessment of the retreat amount. In cases where the shoreline retreat amount is considered to be severe (i.e., 100 m or more, following the same definition used by Vousdoukas et al.3 or when it is less than 100 m, but equals or exceeds the distance from the present-day shoreline to the nearest infrastructure), we flag the location as a sandy beach susceptible to severe future beach loss. The overall workflow is illustrated in Fig. 4. More details are given in the following sections.

Hardened sandy beaches
First, 1 km long shore-normal transects were defined at intervals of 500 m along a global coastline obtained from OSM as shown in Supplementary Fig. 2. On each sandy shore-normal transect, a 90° search quadrant with a 1 km radius was defined, starting at the shoreline (as identified on OSM) (See Supplementary Fig. 2). To define whether a sandy transect is hardened or not, we implemented a logical “AND” condition. This condition requires the presence of both a GISA impervious pixel and an OSM feature within the search sector. Only when this condition is met, we flag the transect as ‘hardened’. These transects are subsequently utilized for global and regional-level quantifications of the percentage of sandy coast that is hardened and may face severe beach loss, based on the presence of GISA and OSM structures within the defined search sector. The distance to the nearest gray infrastructure is computed as an average of the distances to GISA impervious pixel and the OSM feature from the shoreline. As there are no global datasets of sandy beach width available at present, we applied a uniform maximum search distance of 1 km landward from the shoreline to search for any gray infrastructure, and if found, we defined the sandy point as hardened. We performed a sensitivity analysis on the number of hardened structures encountered using different landward search distances. This was done by creating sets of transects with lengths of 250 m, 500 m, and 750 m, generating search sectors with the corresponding radius, and repeating the subsequent steps of searching for gray infrastructure and defining hardened points. The results of our sensitivity analysis indicate that, on a global scale, the increase in the total global hardened coastline percentage is 6% in increasing the search distance from 250 m to 500 m, 4% from 500 m to 750 m, and 3% from 750 m to 1 km (Supplementary Fig. 3). At a regional level too, convergence is reached between 750 m and 1 km search distances, with difference of 0%–5% in computed regional percentage of hardened coastline (For smaller search distances, the difference per 250 m increase in search radius can be up to 12%) (Supplementary Fig. 3).

Severe sandy beach loss projections
At hardened sandy locations, we used the 500 m alongshore resolution shoreline retreat projections from Vousdoukas et al.’s3 to identify locations that may face severe beach loss. A sandy and hardened location is classified as a severe beach loss location if the projected retreat value is (a) >100 m (i.e., following the definition of severe shoreline retreat adopted by Vousdoukas et al.’s3), or (b) <100 m, but equal or greater than the distance from the present-day shoreline to the nearest artificial hardening structure.

We implemented Monte Carlo simulations to probabilistically determine the percentages of severe beach loss projections at the IPCC AR6 sub-region level. At every sandy, hardened transect in an IPCC AR6 region, 1000 random samples of projected shoreline change were generated based on the probability distribution for that location given in Vousdoukas et al.’s3. These shoreline retreat distributions were then collated and converted to a probability distribution. This distribution represents the percentages of shoreline retreat exceeding 100 m and those that are equal to or greater than the distance from the present-day shoreline to the nearest artificial structure when retreat is <100 m. We then take the median (50th percentile, statistically known as the “expected value”) of this probability distribution in each region as the most likely estimate of the percentage of locations that may experience severe beach loss in that region. In addition, for each IPCC AR6 region, we take the percentage of locations corresponding to the 5th percentile as best-case estimates (i.e., low estimate of percentage of severe beach loss locations); and the percentage of beach loss equal to the 95th percentile as worst-case estimates (i.e., high estimate of percentage of severe beach loss locations).

Limitations
Our global quantification of hardened sandy coasts and projections of sandy beaches that may face severe beach loss have certain unavoidable limitations due to the input data and methodological assumptions, which are discussed below. It is important that these limitations are taken into account when considering our results.

Firstly, our results do not include possible future changes in the exposure data, i.e., future changes in gray coastal infrastructure. We also could not project total beach loss since the actual sandy beach width per transect is unknown at a global scale. We acknowledge the possibility of locations where gray infrastructure might exist landward of the shoreline retreat threshold of 100 m used here. At such locations, although severe beach loss may not occur within the time horizons considered in this study, as there is a committed SLR for centuries to come, severe beach loss may occur at some point beyond our limited time horizon. For that reason, we included such locations in our quantification of severe beach loss projections.

Another limitation arises from the input datasets utilized to identify hardened sandy locations. Although GISA-10m demonstrates robust performance in urban settings, its accuracy is lower in rural and arid areas22. To address this limitation and enhance the precision of identifying hardened objects in coastal areas, we integrated community-contributed OSM data. Despite these efforts, there are still globally unmapped areas, notably prevalent in low and lower-middle-income countries. This incompleteness may impact our assessment of hardened coastlines and, consequently, our projections for sandy beach loss, potentially underestimating the extent of hardened sandy coastlines within these under-mapped regions.

Similarly, the stated limitations inherent in the shoreline retreat projections from Vousdoukas et al.’s3 consequently propagate into our assessment of locations that may experience severe sandy beach loss in the future. As mentioned before (see Methods), these retreat projections are the combination of two components: AC (retreat estimated by extrapolating the shoreline dynamics over the past 32 years into the future) and R (retreat due to sea level rise). The fact that AC was derived from dynamics over 32 years cannot fully capture changes caused by rare extreme weather events or substantial human interventions. Moreover, the spatial resolution of the underlying satellite images to compute the AC component, set at 30 m, might be insufficient to detect smaller changes in less energetic areas.

Sandy Beach locations are here taken from Luijendijk et al.’s33 SDS database. Over time, some discrepancies have been noted in this SDS dataset where non-sandy locations had been identified as sandy locations. While, in our study, we removed such known contentious locations from the analysis, there may still be others that we had not removed. It must be recognized that when performing very large-scale assessments such as that done here, which are essential for macroscale decision-making, some local scale imperfections necessarily need to be accepted.

Summary
R2.1 This paper investigates global sandy shorelines and quantifies the proportion of these
shorelines that are hardened (backed by infrastructure/buildings) within a 1km search grid. It
quantifies the proportion of all sandy beaches and hardened sandy beaches that are at risk of
severe beach loss (erosion of >100 m) by mid and end of the century according to data from
Vousdoukas et al. 2020. Lastly, the study categorizes these values based on IPCC AR6 reference
regions and the income groupings from the World Bank.
It is overall a large undertaking of data curation and analysis at a global scale and generally well
documented. However, some further clarification on a few areas could improve the manuscript.

R2.2 My primary concern is the close resemblance of this paper to the study published by Lansu
et al. in Nature Communications in January 2024. While I realize this publication may have
been just before the submission of this paper, I am not sure that I see how this current paper
contributes differently than what has already been published. From my understanding, I’ve
added a very brief comparison on the methodology below for reference:
Lansu et al. 2024 uses the same dataset from Luijendijk et al. 2018 to identify locations of sandy
beaches, then uses the same dataset on shoreline change projections by Vousdoukas et al. 2020
(but at 1000m increments instead of 500m used here), and lastly uses the same OSM dataset as
used here to determine coastal hardening. Although here, the Global impervious surface area
(GISA) raster dataset is primarily used with OSM as a complement to these data, providing an
alternative way to determine coastal hardening. Analysis by Lansu et al. is categorized by
countries, whereas this is categorized by IPCC AR6 reference regions. The overall conclusions
are similar - both studies find 33% global sandy beaches to be hardened. Lansu et al. finds 23%
(30%) of beaches to be lost by the end of the 21st century under RCP4.5 (RPC 8.5). The current
study considers ‘severe’ beach loss and finds 18% (24%) of beaches to likely face severe beach
loss by the end of the 21st century under SSP2-4.5 (SSP5-8.5). Interestingly, Lansu et al. 2024,
with their method of coastal hardening, find a median distance of infrastructure free space to be
392 meters, while this papers find it to be 93 meters.
We thank the Reviewer for the well-researched and detailed comparison with the study by Lansu et al.
(2024). As the Reviewer has guessed, both studies were conducted independently and simultaneously,
without knowledge of each other. In fact, we became aware of Lansu et al's work almost at the
completion of our work (which spanned 18 months from beginning to end). This was very unfortunate
timing. However, as we had seen other very similar papers being published a few months apart in
Nature Portfolio journals, without mentioning each other (e.g. Luijendijk et al., 2018; Mentaschi et al,
2018 - https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-018-24630-6, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-
018-30904-w), we decided to go ahead and submit our paper without comparing and contrasting with
Lansu et al (2024).
As the Reviewer has noted, there are some similarities between Lansu et al. (2024) and our study;
however, there are also significant differences in aims, methodological details, and results. Below we
outline the main differences, highlighting how both studies stand on their own merits:
• While Lansu et al. (2024) focus on investigating coastal squeeze, our study’s final goal is to
provide robust and fully probabilistic projections of sandy beaches that can face 'severe beach
loss'. Lansu et al. (2024) discussed the median value of the projected sandy beach loss using
only the 50th percentile from Vousdoukas et al. (2020) shoreline projections, and only briefly
discussed their results in the Supplementary Information. Our projections are fully
probabilistic, utilizing the complete distribution of shoreline retreat projections from
Vousdoukas et al. (2020).
• Lansu et al. (2024) utilized 1 km spacing along the global coastline for their analysis. In
contrast, we employed 500 m spacing. While more computationally intensive and time
consuming, this finer resolution allowed us to achieve more definitive results. As noted by the
Reviewer, we found the global median distance from the present-day shoreline to the nearest
grey infrastructure to be 93 meters, compared to Lansu et al.'s 392 meters; a large difference.
• Lansu et al. (2024) focused only on paved streets from OSM and buildings from the Global
Urban Footprint (12 m resolution), excluding unpaved seawalls and dikes. In our study, we
included any object defined as a grey structure in the OSM data (including buildings,
transport, and land use) that can obstruct shoreline retreat and the landward translation of
sandy beaches. Additionally, we utilized three versions of the Global Impervious Surface Area
(GISA) dataset with different resolutions (10 m and 30 m). This more detailed analysis
allowed us to better detect any grey structure that would obstruct shoreline retreat and beach
translation.
• As the Reviewer has noted, Lansu et al. (2024) presented their results by countries or
continents, whereas we present our results in terms of IPCC AR6 reference regions.
Based on these facts, we believe that while both studies contribute valuable insights into the topic, the
differences in methodology, focus, and resolution underscore the unique contributions of each study.
We respect the efforts of Lansu et al. (2024) and believe that presenting our work independently
allows both studies to stand on their own merits and provide complementary perspectives on this
important issue of the future of global sandy beaches. We, however, feel a bit uncomfortable including
the above points in a revised manuscript, because such a methodological comparison will most likely
be construed by the authors of Lansu et al. (2024) as a harsh criticism of their work, which is not how
we like to do science. Also, please note that both teams are based in the Netherlands, and we would
not like to antagonize a fellow Dutch team, if we can help it. Therefore, we hope that the above
clarifications help the Reviewer to appreciate the differences between the two seemingly similar
studies, and that it would not be necessary to include such a comparison in our revised manuscript. As
we are facing this issue now, we were very pleased to come across a 2020 editorial in NCOMMs that
specifically addressed similar dilemmas (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-020-17817-x).
